source_evidence.anchor: E1 — Remark 2.7.9 (MGF near the origin), opening paragraph and displayed Taylor approximation
source_evidence.observation: The remark considers a general random variable X with mean zero and unit variance, assumes X is bounded for simplicity, and informally displays, as λ → 0, E exp(λX) ≈ E[1 + λX + λ²X²/2 + o(λ²X²)] = 1 + λ²/2 ≈ exp(λ²/2).

source_evidence.anchor: E2 — Remark 2.7.9, continuation beginning “becomes an equality”
source_evidence.observation: The remark says the normal approximation is exact for N(0,1); a quadratic-exponential MGF bound holds for all λ and characterizes sub-gaussian distributions, while a corresponding bound for small λ characterizes sub-exponential distributions; it also says that no general large-λ bound need exist and gives X ∼ Exp(1), whose MGF is infinite for λ ≥ 1.
For X ∼ N(0,1), E exp(λX) = exp(λ²/2) for every λ ∈ ℝ.

Under E X = 0, the sub-gaussian properties are equivalent to existence of K5 > 0 such that E exp(λX) ≤ exp(K5²λ²) for all λ ∈ ℝ; the parameters in the equivalent properties agree up to an absolute constant factor.

Under E X = 0, the sub-exponential properties are equivalent to existence of K5 > 0 such that E exp(λX) ≤ exp(K5²λ²) whenever |λ| ≤ 1/K5; the parameters in the equivalent properties agree up to an absolute constant factor.

source_evidence.anchor: E6 — Example 2.7.8, definition of the exponential distribution
source_evidence.observation: The source uses X ∼ Exp(r) for a nonnegative random variable satisfying P{X ≥ t} = exp(−rt) for t ≥ 0 and rate r > 0; hence Exp(1) in the remark is the rate-one exponential law.

contract_plain_english: Remark 2.7.9 gives a heuristic local picture of MGFs. For a bounded random variable with mean zero and variance one, its MGF near λ = 0 is approximated by the constant, linear, and quadratic Taylor terms; centering kills the linear term and unit variance leaves 1 + λ²/2, which is itself close to exp(λ²/2). The standard normal has exp(λ²/2) exactly for every real λ. More generally, a centered sub-gaussian variable is characterized by some quadratic-exponential MGF upper bound valid for all real λ, while a centered sub-exponential variable is characterized by such a bound only in a neighborhood of zero. Large-parameter finiteness can fail: the rate-one exponential law has infinite MGF for λ ≥ 1. [E1–E6 — Remark 2.7.9, equation (2.12), Propositions 2.5.2(v) and 2.7.1(e), and Example 2.7.8]
